items.title: Small Area Deprivation and Depression or Anxiety in a Nationwide Cohort.
items.authors: Johansson EW, Ohlis A, Mattsson M, Shaaban AN, Gardner RM, Wicks S, Agardh EE.

sections.heading: Importance
sections.text: Prior studies suggest increased risk of mental health conditions in deprived residential areas, but robust evidence leveraging nationwide health care and prescription registers, including primary care, with socioeconomic databases is lacking.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To examine the association between small-area deprivation and depression or anxiety in people aged 10 to 50 years without recent history of these conditions.

sections.heading: Design, setting, and participants
sections.text: This nationwide register-based cohort study with sibling analysis was conducted in Sweden January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2023, with analysis completed in January to September 2026. Participants were registered in Sweden throughout the study period, including siblings with discordant-exposure status.

sections.heading: Exposure
sections.text: Small-area deprivation in 2015 was defined for 5984 areas using an Index for Multiple Deprivation in Sweden categorized into quartiles.

sections.heading: Main outcomes and measures
sections.text: Depression or anxiety was defined as the first diagnosis or the first prescription date if no diagnosis was recorded in the study period. Hazard ratios (HRs) for the outcome through December 31, 2023, were computed using Cox regression models adjusted for confounders. Sibling analyses used stratified Cox regression with robust error variance. We separately tested for interactions between small-area deprivation and age, sex, and urbanicity in the association with the outcome.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 4 065 375 participants (2 169 625 male [53.4%]; median [IQR] age, 30 [20-41] years), including 1 301 647 siblings, were included. Incidence rates per 1000 person-years for depression or anxiety varied across deprivation levels from 22.8 (95% CI, 22.7-22.9; very low) to 25.6 (95% CI, 25.5-25.7; very high). The HR for depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived area was 1.18 (95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and 1.15 (95% CI, 1.13-1.17) in the sibling cohort. Urban (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and periurban (HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.18-1.23) residents in most vs least deprived areas had higher depression or anxiety rates than rural counterparts (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.08-1.14).

sections.heading: Conclusions and relevance
sections.text: In this study, people in the most vs least deprived areas had increased depression or anxiety rates, and the association remained in sibling comparisons. There were increased rates of depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived areas of urban and periurban settings compared with rural settings, potentially reflecting worse outcomes in deprived urban areas or less contact with mental health services in remote and rural areas.

items.title: Prevalence of depression and anxiety among patients with Behçet's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.authors: Mehrpoor G, Amini MJ, Shafiee A, Salehi SA, Samiee R, Azarinoush G.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Behçet's disease (BD) is a chronic multisystemic vasculitis associated with significant physical and psychological morbidity, including depression and anxiety. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of depression and anxiety among BD patients and to examine variations by assessment tools and geographic regions.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus was conducted up to April 2025. Data were extracted and quality-assessed using standardized tools, and pooled prevalence rates were calculated via random-effects meta-analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 17 studies were included in the systematic review, of which 16 contributed to the meta-analysis of depression and 11 to the meta-analysis of anxiety among patients with BD. The results revealed a high pooled prevalence of depression at 47.44% (95% CI: 34.09-60.97%) and anxiety at 48.48% (95% CI: 35.40-61.67%), both with substantial heterogeneity (I² > 90%). Depression prevalence varied significantly by diagnostic instrument, with PHQ-9 and HADS reporting higher rates compared to DSM-IV and MINI. Geographic differences were marked, with Egypt showing the highest prevalence for both depression (88.83%) and anxiety (92.00%), while France reported the lowest prevalence for depression (5.00%) and Brazil reported the lowest for anxiety (29.31%). No publication bias was detected.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The findings underscore a high burden of mental health comorbidities in BD, with pooled prevalence rates of 47.44% for depression and 48.48% for anxiety, reflecting significant psychological morbidity. Geographic disparities, suggest cultural, healthcare, or socioeconomic moderators requiring further investigation. These results advocate for integrating routine mental health screening into BD management to address unmet psychiatric needs in this population.

items.title: Patterns of antidepressant persistence in mood and anxiety disorders: a retrospective population-based cohort study.
items.authors: Aziz MA, Al Maruf A, Bolton JM, Kowalec K, Eltonsy S, Friesen K, Leong C.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Controlled studies and practice guidelines encourage antidepressant treatment to be continued for at least 6 to 12 months after symptom remission to reduce the risk of relapses. We aimed to assess the real-world persistence of prescribed antidepressants and identify factors affecting long-term persistence.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective cohort study used outpatient prescription dispensing data from 2015 to 2021. The baseline and follow-up periods were set as 12 months before and after the index date, respectively. Administrative health data for this were obtained from the Population Health Research Data Repository at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy in Manitoba, Canada. Individuals covered by the Manitoba Health Insurance Registry who initiated an antidepressant prescription and had a diagnosis of mood and anxiety disorders were included. The proportion of individuals who persisted on their first antidepressant prescription was determined at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months, and the odds of persistence were determined using multivariable logistic regression models.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among 76,200 new antidepressant users (63.3% female), 30.2% of individuals filled their first antidepressant prescription only once, and 75.4% of users discontinued within 1 year. The proportion of individuals who persisted with their initial antidepressants declined over 3, 6, 9, and 12 months (56%, 41%, 33%, and 25%, respectively). Adjusted analyses identified several predictors of lower persistence at 12 months, including male sex (vs. female: OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.84-0.90), younger age (< 25 years vs. 25-65 years: OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.71-0.77), receipt of income assistance (vs. no assistance: OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.53-0.61), receiving tricyclic antidepressants (vs. receiving SSRIs: OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.28-0.34), concurrent benzodiazepine use (vs. non-use: OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.84-0.91), prior PTSD diagnosis (vs. no PTSD: OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.76-0.91), and mood and anxiety-related ambulatory visits (vs. no visits: OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88-0.95).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Antidepressant persistence among individuals with mood and anxiety disorders declined over time after the initial prescription and varied by demographic, clinical, and healthcare utilization factors. These findings underscore the need to identify individuals at higher risk of discontinuation and support further research to inform clinical and health system strategies to improve persistence.

items.title: Phase-sensitive integration of motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders: a scoping review.
items.authors: Ho MH, Okoli C, Tung CL, Hong RM.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for anxiety disorders; however, treatment engagement, adherence, and premature dropout remain persistent clinical challenges. Motivational interviewing (MI) has increasingly been integrated with CBT to address ambivalence, enhance treatment readiness, and support treatment engagement across different phases of therapy. This scoping review mapped and synthesized existing models of MI-CBT integration and their reported clinical and methodological characteristics.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2005 and December 2025. Eligible studies examined integrated MI-CBT interventions for anxiety disorders. Data were synthesized descriptively. Based on recurrent implementation patterns identified across the included studies, a preliminary conceptual synthesis was developed to organize MI-CBT integration according to treatment sequencing, phase-specific engagement functions, delivery formats, and implementation characteristics.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Nine empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Three broad MI-CBT integration approaches were identified: pretreatment MI, concurrent/embedded MI, and intermittent/responsive MI. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across studies in treatment sequencing, MI content, dosage, therapist training, fidelity monitoring, and implementation procedures. Across studies, MI was primarily implemented with the reported aim of enhancing and address motivational challenges, with several studies reported improved in treatment readiness, adherence, attendance, therapeutic alliance, and resistance management. Evidence for incremental symptom improvement beyond standard CBT remained inconsistent.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Based on recurrent descriptive patterns identified across the included studies, a preliminary conceptual framework was developed to organize the observed MI-CBT integration approaches. The reviewed literature suggests that MI may have potential value for addressing ambivalence, strengthening the therapeutic alliance, managing resistance, and supporting engagement during clinically challenging phases of CBT. However, the current evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous. Future research should evaluate this preliminary conceptual framework across diverse clinical populations and implementation settings while clarifying optimal sequencing strategies, fidelity procedures, dosage parameters, and the role of therapist-supported and asynchronous digital CBT interventions.

items.title: Alcohol use and its associations with mental health across the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.
items.authors: Zhang L, Ton B, Mewton L, Schweizer S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: While the COVID-19 pandemic caused major disruptions to social connections and lifestyles, many countries continued the sale of alcohol as an essential commodity. Evidence on change in alcohol use, and its association with mental health and wellbeing during the pandemic is, however, mixed and limited to initial periods of the pandemic. This study aimed to address these research gaps.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Data were drawn from the COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study, a three-wave longitudinal study conducted between May 2020 and April 2021. The present sample included 2,369 participants (ageM = 38.81 ± 16.94 years, range = 11-100; 90% females) from the United Kingdom, United States, and Australia. Measures included pre-pandemic alcohol use and changes in consumption frequency, quantity, drinking behaviours (e.g., drinking earlier in the day), and motivations (e.g., drinking for enjoyment) during the pandemic. General perceived stress, COVID-19-related stress, loneliness, and symptoms of depression and anxiety were also assessed.

sections.heading: Findings
sections.text: Drinking frequency and quantity remained stable across the first year of the pandemic; however, non-linear age associations were found. Young individuals aged between 11 to 20 years, and mid-aged individuals aged between 50 to 70 years, had the highest probability of increased alcohol use frequency and quantity. Drinking behaviours and motivations also remained largely stable, although age- and country-specific differences emerged, potentially reflecting policy differences such as alcohol access restrictions and lockdown measures. Finally, loneliness unidirectionally predicted subsequent alcohol use quantity.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: These findings highlight the heterogeneous alcohol use patterns across age groups and countries during the pandemic, and underscore loneliness as an important public health issue with implications for alcohol misuse.

items.title: Defeating fear with exposure therapy delivered by mental health nurses in primary care for anxiety disorders in older adults: a protocol for a cluster-randomized controlled trial (DeFEAD65+).
items.authors: Baturlar Ö, Rijkelijkhuizen-Haffmans DNJ, Ikani N, Collard R, Hartman TO, Janssen N, Voshaar RO, Schers H, Bosmans JE, Meijel BV, Kampman M, Becker E, Kool T, Hendriks GJ.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Anxiety disorders are associated with a high disease burden throughout the life span. Anxiety disorders in older adults, however, remain frequently untreated, and when treated, pharmacotherapy predominates despite age-related risks and a preference for psychotherapy. Exposure Therapy is the most effective intervention for anxiety disorders and is a suitable treatment method to be delivered in primary care centres by mental health nurses. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the (cost-) effectiveness of ET delivered by trained MHNs compared to usual care in reducing anxiety symptoms and improving quality of life among older adults with anxiety disorders in primary care. The secondary objective is to examine secondary outcomes, including comorbid depressive symptoms and disorder-specific anxiety symptoms. We also aim to investigate potential predictors and moderators of treatment outcome, as well as possible mechanisms of change in exposure therapy for older adults with anxiety disorders.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A multi-centre cluster-randomised controlled trial conducted in primary care with two parallel groups: (a) exposure therapy, and (b) usual care, with one-year follow-up. Participants must meet the criteria for a primary Diagnostics and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition anxiety disorder. Exclusion criteria are earlier treatment for anxiety disorder, other somatic and/or psychiatric morbidity that could interfere with diagnostics or treatment, being terminally ill, and having a moderate to severe cognitive impairment and stable pharmacotherapy use. The intervention consists of eight 30-min ET sessions delivered over 12 weeks. Primary outcome measures are anxiety severity as assessed with the Geriatric Anxiety Inventory, societal costs as assessed with the Trimbos and iMTA questionnaire on Costs associated with Psychiatric illness, and quality of life using the EuroQol 5 Dimension 5 Level version.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Even though participating in present study involves a time investment for patients, we expect that they will benefit from the offered exposure therapy in a more effective way than usual care, as we anticipate a beneficial impact on their anxiety symptoms. If proven effective, exposure therapy could represent a valuable addition to existing clinical guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders in older adults within primary care settings.

sections.heading: Trial registration
sections.text: This study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06770517) on 26 February 2025.

Anxiety disorders in older adults, however, remain frequently untreated, and when treated, pharmacotherapy predominates despite age-related risks and a preference for psychotherapy. Exposure Therapy is the most effective intervention for anxiety disorders and is a suitable treatment method to be delivered in primary care centres by mental health nurses. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the (cost-) effectiveness of ET delivered by trained MHNs compared to usual care in reducing anxiety symptoms and improving quality of life among older adults with anxiety disorders in primary care. The secondary objective is to examine secondary outcomes, including comorbid depressive symptoms and disorder-specific anxiety symptoms. We also aim to investigate potential predictors and moderators of treatment outcome, as well as possible mechanisms of change in exposure therapy for older adults with anxiety disorders.

A multi-centre cluster-randomised controlled trial conducted in primary care with two parallel groups: (a) exposure therapy, and (b) usual care, with one-year follow-up. Participants must meet the criteria for a primary Diagnostics and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition anxiety disorder. Exclusion criteria are earlier treatment for anxiety disorder, other somatic and/or psychiatric morbidity that could interfere with diagnostics or treatment, being terminally ill, and having a moderate to severe cognitive impairment and stable pharmacotherapy use. The intervention consists of eight 30-min ET sessions delivered over 12 weeks. Primary outcome measures are anxiety severity as assessed with the Geriatric Anxiety Inventory, societal costs as assessed with the Trimbos and iMTA questionnaire on Costs associated with Psychiatric illness, and quality of life using the EuroQol 5 Dimension 5 Level version.

Even though participating in present study involves a time investment for patients, we expect that they will benefit from the offered exposure therapy in a more effective way than usual care, as we anticipate a beneficial impact on their anxiety symptoms. If proven effective, exposure therapy could represent a valuable addition to existing clinical guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders in older adults within primary care settings.

This study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06770517) on 26 February 2025.

items.title: The relationship between techno-distress and well-being among university students: the moderating effects of positive youth development attributes and techno-stressors.
items.authors: Huang C, Xia X, Dou D, Li J.

sections.text: This study investigated the relationships between techno-distress and university students' well-being and examined the moderating roles of positive youth development (PYD) and techno-stressors. Data were collected from 636 university students in mainland China (36.95% male; M_age = 21.24; SD_age = 1.43) via an online questionnaire. Hierarchical regressions with dual moderators were conducted using PROCESS Macro v4.2, controlling for digital literacy and organizational support. The findings revealed that techno-distress was positively associated with academic burnout and depression and negatively correlated with life satisfaction. Overall, PYD did not demonstrate a significant moderating role; however, among students with higher levels of competence-related PYD subdimensions, techno-distress was less strongly related to adverse mental health outcomes. In contrast, overall techno-stressors significantly amplified the relationship between techno-distress and depression, particularly under the dimensions of techno-complexity, techno-insecurity, and techno-uncertainty. These findings highlight the dimension-specific patterns in the moderating role of PYD and indicate that association between techno-distress and mental health outcomes was stronger under higher levels of environmental demands. This study contributes to stress theory by providing a precise technostress framework and offers practical recommendations for reducing techno-distress in higher education.

items.title: Effect of Blonanserin on Neurotrophic Factors in Patients With Non-Responsive First-Episode Schizophrenia Treated With Early Risperidone Monotherapy-A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.authors: Wei Y, Liu Y, Cai L, Li J, Zheng D, Fu H, Wang S, Huang G.
items.journal: International journal of methods in psychiatric research

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To investigate the efficacy of Blonanserin in patients with schizophrenia who were refractory to Risperidone monotherapy and its effects on various neurotrophic factors.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 120 patients with first-episode schizophrenia who were hospitalized in our hospital from January 2022 to December 2023 and did not respond to early Risperidone monotherapy were selected as the study participants. They were randomly divided into a control group and a research group, with 60 cases in each group. The control group was treated with Clozapine, and the research group was treated with Blonanserin for 3 months. The scores of the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), the scores of the Generic Quality of Life Inventory (GQOLI-74), the serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), the serum S100β protein, the neuron-specific enolase (NSE), and the Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) levels of the two groups were compared, and the adverse drug reactions of patients were recorded.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: After 3 months of treatment, the PANSS scores of both groups decreased compared with those before treatment, and the PANSS scores of the research group were lower. The scores of physical function, social function, and psychological function of the two groups were higher than those before treatment, and the scores of the research group were higher than those of the control group. The differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05 for all). The serum BDNF and NRG1 levels of the two groups were higher than those before treatment, and those of the research group were higher than those of the control group. The S100β and NSE levels of the two groups were lower than those before treatment, and those of the research group were lower than those of the control group. The differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05 for all). No serious adverse reactions occurred in both groups. Most patients with adverse reactions could tolerate them or improved after symptomatic treatment.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Blonanserin can effectively relieve the symptoms of schizophrenia and improve the quality of life of first-episode schizophrenia patients who have failed to respond to Risperidone monotherapy in the early stage. Due to the short follow-up time and small sample size of this study, further prospective multicenter studies should be carried out in the future to observe the long-term treatment effect and provide more favorable reference for clinical practice.

items.title: Early childhood serum and urine metabolite signatures of internalizing, externalizing, and ADHD traits and their trajectories to adolescence: the Rhea mother-child cohort.
items.authors: Barmpa E, Koutra K, Mouatsou C, Margetaki K, Kampouri M, Konopidou A, Chatziioannou AC, Tsilidis KK, Vrijheid M, Maitre L, Keun HC, Kogevinas M, Karachaliou M, Papandreou C.
items.journal: Metabolomics : Official journal of the Metabolomic Society

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Early-life emotional and behavioral difficulties increase vulnerability to later psychopathology, but it remains unclear whether a biological footprint is detectable in early childhood.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: We aimed to identify serum- and urine-based metabolite signatures of internalizing, externalizing, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits in 6-year-old children and examine their associations with traits through adolescence.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We analyzed 196 participants of the Rhea cohort (Greece), with serum and urine metabolomics at age 6 and internalizing, externalizing, and ADHD traits assessed at ages 6, 11, and 15. Trait- and biofluid-specific metabolite signatures were identified using elastic net regression with cross-validation. Associations with subsequent traits at repeated time points were evaluated using confounder-adjusted linear mixed-effects models.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Metabolite signatures comprising amino acids, acylcarnitines, phosphatidylcholines, and gut microbiota-related metabolites were identified for internalizing, externalizing, and ADHD traits. Serum metabolite scores were associated with increased internalizing (β = 0.40; 95% CI 0.14-0.68) and externalizing traits (β = 0.83; 95% CI 0.56-1.1). Urine metabolite scores were associated with internalizing (β = 0.42; 95% CI 0.16-0.68) and externalizing traits (β = 0.69; 95% CI 0.43-0.95), while the association with ADHD traits was nominal (β = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.006-0.502; nominal p = 0.045; BH-FDR p = 0.054). Associations were stable over time for internalizing and ADHD but weakened with age for externalizing traits.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This proof-of-concept study shows that complementary serum and urine metabolomic profiles in early childhood are associated with subsequent internalizing and externalizing trait trajectories, while a nominal longitudinal association was observed between the urine metabolite profile and ADHD traits. These findings warrant evaluation in larger independent studies.

items.title: Persistent Amotivation After Cannabis-Related Psychosis: Diagnostic Challenges and Clinical Course With Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Case Report.
items.authors: Kitano Y, Takada R, Ikehara M, Yamanaka K, Sunami Y, Okada T.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Cannabis use may cause psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions, as well as persistent amotivation with reduced motivation, inactivity, and cognitive impairment. Although described as cannabis-related amotivational syndrome, it is not recognized as an independent diagnostic entity and overlaps clinically with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and mood disorders. We report a case of persistent amotivation following cannabis-related psychosis that improved after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

sections.heading: Case
sections.text: A 19-year-old man developed auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and agitation associated with cannabis use and was admitted to a psychiatric hospital. Antipsychotic treatment improved the psychotic symptoms, but marked amotivation and inactivity, accompanied by low performance on cognitive screening, and significantly impaired daily functioning. Depressed mood and appetite loss were not evident. Although negative symptoms of schizophrenia remained a differential diagnosis, the presentation was consistent with cannabis-related amotivational syndrome. Amantadine produced limited improvement. Following ECT, the Apathy Scale score improved from 24 to 7 and the Mini-Mental State Examination score increased from 19 to 26, with improvements in motivation, activity, and daily functioning.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This case demonstrates that clinically significant amotivation may persist after cannabis-related psychotic symptoms improve. Persistently reduced motivation and inactivity should not be assumed to represent primary negative symptoms of schizophrenia; rather, clinicians should carefully consider mood symptoms and cannabis-related amotivation in the differential diagnosis. This case also suggests that ECT may represent a treatment option for severe, persistent amotivation following cannabis-related psychosis. However, because this was a single case, further validation through additional cases and long-term follow-up is required.

items.title: Reading Skills and Reading Anxiety Symptoms in Youth.
items.authors: Handsman R, Rozenman M, Christodoulou JA, Pennington BF, Willcutt EG, McGrath LM.
items.journal: Research on child and adolescent psychopathology

sections.text: Many children who experience reading challenges develop co-occurring mental health difficulties, such as reading anxiety. The current study tested the relationships between specific reading skills (decoding, fluency, and comprehension) and reading anxiety symptoms. Participants were 230 twins between 8 and 13 years old. Multi-level linear regression models were used to account for family relationships and covaried for age and sex. Age was positively associated and sex was not associated with reading anxiety. Lower decoding (β = -0.19, p <.001), reading fluency (β = -0.22, p <.001), and reading comprehension skills (β = -0.22, p <.001) were significantly associated with higher reading anxiety symptoms. When testing whether each reading skill contributed to reading anxiety after controlling for others, reading comprehension (β = -0.15, p =.010) remained significantly associated with reading anxiety symptoms, whereas decoding (β = 0.01, p =.90) and reading fluency (β = -0.13, p = .08) were no longer significant. Model comparisons followed a similar pattern indicating that reading comprehension (and to a lesser extent fluency) accounted for significant variance in reading anxiety over and above other reading skills, while decoding did not. Secondary analyses covarying for clinical anxiety and ADHD symptoms showed that the association between reading skills and reading anxiety could not be accounted for by these co-occurring symptoms. This study is among the first to examine relationships between specific reading skills and reading anxiety symptoms and highlights the need for improved identification and treatment of reading anxiety symptoms in struggling readers.

items.title: Transdiagnostic metacognitive therapy compared to disorder-specific cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders: a study protocol for a randomized controlled superiority trial.
items.authors: Petersén N, Santoft F, Jayaram-Lindström N, Jansson-Fröjmark M, Alfonsson S, Bohman B.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent worldwide and are associated with functional impairment, reduced quality of life and high societal costs. With only approximately 50% of patients achieving remission following cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), the evaluation of other effective treatments is warranted. Studies suggest that metacognitive therapy (MCT) may be more effective than CBT for anxiety disorders. Although transdiagnostic treatment may be beneficial for treatment implementation and dissemination in routine care, there is currently only one adequately powered study comparing transdiagnostic MCT (tMCT) to disorder-specific CBT for anxiety disorders. The main aim of this trial is to investigate the effectiveness of tMCT compared to disorder-specific CBT for anxiety disorders. The trial also aims to investigate potential mediators of treatment effects in tMCT and CBT, to conduct a health economic evaluation and to explore patients' perspectives on the treatments.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This trial is a prospective, pragmatic, two-arm parallel-group randomized controlled superiority trial comparing tMCT with disorder-specific CBT, conducted in outpatient psychiatric services in Stockholm, Sweden. A sample of 86 adults with a principal diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder or posttraumatic stress disorder will be recruited and randomly allocated to tMCT or CBT. Primary outcomes are self-rated symptoms of principal diagnosis, and secondary outcomes are clinical severity, remission rates, depressive symptoms, functional impairment and quality of life. Outcomes will be assessed at pre- and post-treatment as well as at 6- and 12-month follow-up. Metacognitions and cognitions as potential mediators will be measured weekly during treatment. Cost-effectiveness of tMCT compared to CBT will be investigated. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted with participants from both conditions.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Considering the potential of MCT, further research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness compared to CBT, particularly MCT in a transdiagnostic format. Results from this trial will add to the evidence base for tMCT and inform treatment development, decision-making and implementation of effective treatment for anxiety disorders in routine care.

items.title: Sex differences in the association between Hcy levels and cognitive deficits among individuals with first-episode and drug-naive major depressive disorder.
items.authors: Zhou S, Huang Y, Feng S, Li H, Zhang Z, Liu C, Li J, Han W, Wu K, Huang X, Wu F.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Previous studies have shown that elevated homocysteine (Hcy) levels are associated with cognitive deficits in first-episode and drug-naive individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD). However, research on sex differences in this context is limited. This study aimed to evaluate sex differences in the association between Hcy levels and cognitive deficits among individuals with first-episode and drug-naive MDD.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We recruited 85 MDD patients and 100 healthy controls. The MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB) was used to assess cognitive function, and serum Hcy levels were measured in all participants. Clinical features, including affective and psychotic symptom dimensions, were evaluated using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Hcy levels were significantly higher in male patients with MDD than in female patients (Z = 3.58, P = 0.001). Female patients had significantly higher PANSS positive symptoms (F = 2.06, P = 0.043) and speed of processing (SOP) scores (F = 2.02, P = 0.047) than male patients. In male patients, higher Hcy levels were found to be positively correlated with the severity of positive symptoms (r = 0.477, P = 0.010) and correlated with working memory (WM) scores (r = -0.409, P = 0.030). Additionally, in male patients with MDD, multivariate regression analyses revealed that Hcy levels were independent predictors of WM scores (B = -0.43, t = 2.37, P = 0.026) and positive symptoms (B = 0.14, t = 2.42, P = 0.024).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: These findings highlight that Hcy levels differ between the sexes, and that in males, MDD Hcy levels were significantly associated with the severity of positive symptoms and cognitive deficits. These results support the potential of Hcy as a biomarker for cognitive deficits and positive psychotic symptoms, which provide a target for therapeutic intervention in male patients with MDD.

items.title: The relationship between dietary nutrient intake and adolescent depression based on the dietary inflammation index: a case-control study.
items.authors: Cheng J, Ma N, Liu Q, Yang G, Ma C, Han H, Liu N, Liu Z, Han S.

sections.heading: Background and purpose
sections.text: The global increase in adolescent Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) has profound implications for physical and mental development, contributing to a significant societal burden. Emerging evidence suggests that low-grade chronic inflammation, commonly observed in adolescents with MDD, is associated with the severity of the disorder. This study explores the relationship among dietary inflammation, dietary nutrients and adolescent depression, utilizing data from the Energy-adjusted Dietary Inflammatory Index (E-DII) in a population from northern China.

sections.heading: Methods

sections.text: Digital mental health technologies hold promise, yet their integration into routine care remains challenging. This study reports findings from an implementation workshop conducted midway through an ongoing multi-site randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating a smartphone-based relapse prevention app for patients with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Sixteen stakeholders, including developers, researchers, and clinicians, discussed experiences and barriers using a semi-structured agenda, incorporating prior feedback from three focus groups with people with lived experience, and analyzed the discussions using an adopted R(E)-AIM framework (Reach, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance). Findings highlight the need for structural, technical, and personnel adjustments to support sustainable implementation. Key recommendations include integrating digital tools into discharge planning, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration, delegating digital responsibilities, and streamlining technical workflows to facilitate seamless adoption. These insights inform feasibility considerations and strategic requirements for digital interventions in severe mental illness, offering guidance for future RCTs and practice-oriented integration of digital therapeutics in psychiatric care.

items.title: The momentary associations of negative affect, anxiety and stress with symptoms in individuals with anorexia nervosa: a scoping review.
items.authors: Quagebeur R, De Schuyteneer E, Vergaelen E, Presseller EK, Vrieze E.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Negative affect, anxiety, and stress are common in individuals with anorexia nervosa (AN), but their momentary link to symptoms remains unclear. This review aims to (1) examine how negative affect, anxiety, and stress are associated with eating-disorder-related symptoms in the moment in individuals with AN and (2) explore how these concepts are conceptualised and measured across studies in this field.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A systematic search following PRISMA-ScR guidelines was conducted across 11 databases. Eligible studies included individuals with a diagnosis of (atypical) AN, examined negative affect, anxiety, or stress, and reported outcomes related to AN symptoms.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: We identified 95 eligible studies, which we categorised into retrospective self-report, qualitative, experimental, and daily life studies. Across experimental paradigms, negative affect was primarily examined in relation to disorder-specific cognitions. In daily life studies, negative affect was associated with binge eating and purging, while associations with restriction and physical activity were mixed. Mealtime anxiety was related to caloric intake. Stress investigated using general stress paradigms yielded mixed findings for eating-disorder behaviours, with notable divergences between subjective and physiological stress responses. Few studies directly compared negative affect, anxiety, and stress within the same design, limiting conclusions regarding their relative importance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Negative affect, anxiety and stress are associated with disorder-specific cognitions and urges, though the translation into observable behaviour varies by context and subtype. Future research must address current gaps by adopting multi-modal assessments. Strengthening methodological consistency will be important for advancing the understanding of the interplay between affective states and symptoms in AN.

items.title: National Institutes of Health Funding for Research About Transgender and Nonbinary Youths.
items.authors: Weideman BCD, Parchem B, Reigada T, Rider GN.

sections.heading: Importance
sections.text: Research is needed to improve health and well-being for transgender and nonbinary (TGNB) youths (<18 years), including access to gender-affirming medical care (GAMC) and associated clinical outcomes. Investment in TGNB youth research at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has not been well-characterized even though it has been the source of considerable public debate and recent policy changes to restrict funding.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To examine patterns of funding for TGNB youth research at NIH, including trends over time, demographic subgroups, GAMC and other health topics, and geographic distribution.

sections.heading: Design, setting, and participants
sections.text: This cross-sectional study examined NIH funding for research related to TGNB youths from 2012 to 2024, using the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools (RePORTER) database. Awards were included if abstracts explicitly focused on TGNB youth health. This study took place at the University of Minnesota and used publicly available data regarding domestic and international grants administered by NIH. It did not include participants.

sections.heading: Exposure
sections.text: NIH funding for TGNB youth research.

sections.heading: Main outcomes and measures
sections.text: The amount of TGNB youth awards, both as a total and a proportion of the NIH portfolio was calculated. Award characteristics (eg, administering institute) were extracted from NIH RePORTER, and costs were inflation-adjusted to 2024 dollar values. Systematic coding of abstracts characterized demographic subgroups and health topics for each award.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Between 2012 and 2024, 97 awards and 42 supplements totaling $158.3 million were issued for research about TGNB youths, representing 0.06% of the NIH portfolio. Funding increased over the study period and was concentrated among institutions in states with currently protective GAMC policies. To align funding with estimates of the population size of TGNB youths, investment would need to increase by a factor of 3.5 to 9.8. Nonbinary youths and racially and ethnically minoritized TGNB youths were minimally funded. Common research topics included HIV or AIDS ($68.8 million; 43.5%) and mental health ($78.0 million; 49.3%), with the latter associated with increases in total funding from 2021 onward. GAMC funding ($38.3 million; 24.2%) increased moderately over time.

sections.heading: Conclusions and relevance
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study of NIH awards, research about TGNB youths increased from 2012 to 2024, but it was substantially below population-proportional levels, reflecting historical underfunding and structural barriers in research prioritization.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Evidence-based self-help digital interventions are a promising approach to low-barrier mental health and well-being support. They could be particularly impactful at the early stages of help-seeking and could reach young people who may not otherwise access any help at all. To capitalise on these interventions, they need to be offered in ways that are engaging and easily navigated by the end-user and promote trust and credibility. Co-designing the implementation of these interventions could enable this.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We aimed to co-design a website to host self-help digital interventions aimed at young people in the United Kingdom. We used the Design, Develop, Build and Test model to guide our development process. Over 8 months, we ran a series of participatory virtual co-design workshops with young people as contributors (N = 29, 13-18 years).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: By iteratively moving between the design-development-build phases, we co-created our website, including branding, look and feel, structure, content and functionality. All design decisions were led by what young people told us was most important to them.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Young people's input shaped every aspect of the co-designed unlockwellbeing.org.uk website, from branding to functionality, ensuring relevance, credibility and accessibility.

Using the Design, Develop, Build and Test model, we engaged 29 young people aged 13-18 in a series of virtual workshops over 8 months, ensuring that every design decision, from branding to functionality, was led by their input.

items.title: Teacher-delivered transdiagnostic child mental healthcare in rural Indian primary schools (Tealeaf): study protocol for a batched stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial with a hybrid effectiveness-implementation-context design.
items.authors: Matergia M, Giri P, Rai RP, Lamb M, Pandit D, Bhattarai S, Thapa A, Dukpa C, Lama R, Cruz C.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Mental health conditions affect a substantial proportion of school-aged children in low-resource settings, yet access to evidence-based care remains limited. In rural India, shortages of child mental health specialists, socioeconomic adversity, and structural barriers to care contribute to a large unmet need. Tealeaf is a transdiagnostic model of teacher-delivered mental health care that embeds evidence-based therapeutic techniques into routine classroom interactions. Developed in partnership with communities in the Darjeeling Himalayas, Tealeaf has demonstrated feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness signals. This trial will evaluate its real-world effectiveness and examine implementation and contextual factors influencing care.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We will conduct a hybrid study of effectiveness, implementation, and context using a batched stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial. Schools are organized into two batches, each consisting of multiple sequences. Within each batch, schools begin with enhanced usual care before crossing over to the Tealeaf intervention according to a randomized stepped-wedge schedule. In Tealeaf, teachers are trained to identify children with mental health needs and deliver individualized, transdiagnostic therapeutic strategies throughout the academic year. The primary effectiveness outcome is teacher-reported child mental health status; secondary outcomes include parent-reported symptoms, adaptive functioning, academic achievement, and attendance. Implementation outcomes will be assessed using the RE-AIM framework. A parallel qualitative study will generate contextual understanding through longitudinal ethnography, interviews, participant observation, and field notes. Qualitative analyses will examine how caregiving norms, institutional environments, and social conditions shape perceptions of mental health and influence implementation and variation in outcomes. Quantitative analyses will use mixed-effects models appropriate for batched stepped-wedge designs, with integration of qualitative and quantitative findings to assess contextual moderators of effectiveness and implementation.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This study will generate rigorous evidence on the effectiveness of teacher-delivered, transdiagnostic mental health care in under-resourced school settings, while elucidating how implementation processes and context shape real-world impact.

items.title: Nursing Student Led Blood Pressure Education in a Community Mental Health Setting: A Pre Post Test Study.
items.authors: Stephen C, Yousiph T, Halcomb E, Jay EK, Smith B, Patterson C, Curtis E, Mullan J, Moxham L.
items.journal: International journal of mental health nursing

sections.text: People living with mental illness have greater cardiovascular risk, more lifestyle risk factors and lower health literacy than the general population. The high prevalence of hypertension among people living with mental illness places them at a significantly higher risk of premature morbidity and mortality. Identifying hypertension and empowering consumers to understand its significance are key to controlling elevated blood pressure. Student nurse led blood pressure education in community mental health settings may improve hypertension awareness while building nursing students' confidence and competence. This study sought to evaluate the impact of a preregistration nursing student led blood pressure education activity on consumer blood pressure knowledge and nursing students' health education competence. A single group pre post test intervention study was undertaken during a community mental health clinical placement (Recovery Camp, New South Wales, Australia). Nursing students delivered a brief blood pressure education activity to consumers living with mental illness. Consumer knowledge was assessed using the Hypertension Evaluation of Lifestyle and Management (HELM) scale, and student competence was assessed using the Nurse Health Education Competence Instrument (I-CEpSE). Twenty-one consumers completed paired assessments. Mean HELM scores increased from 5.0 (SD 2.65) pre activity to 6.9 (SD 2.69) post activity (p < 0.001). Forty-four students completed paired assessments, with I-CEpSE total scores increasing from 210.95 (SD 28.81) to 257.27 (SD 30.22) (p < 0.001). This study has demonstrated that a structured, student led blood pressure education activity embedded within a community mental health placement improved both consumer hypertension knowledge and student reported health education competence.

items.title: Multidomain Outcomes of a Digital Self-Management Program in Rural Adults With Chronic Conditions: Single-Arm Prospective Interventional Study.
items.authors: Smith NK, Ilie G, MacDonald C, Langley JRB, Rutledge RDH.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Chronic disease and comorbid mental health problems disproportionately affect rural and underserved populations. Digital self-management programs are potentially scalable, but evaluations often focus on narrow outcomes.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study examined 12-month longitudinal changes in psychological and multidomain outcomes among Pictou County Patient Empowerment Program participants and explored co-occurring changes and psychological moderators.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This single-arm prospective interventional study enrolled 182 community-dwelling adults with ≥1 chronic condition in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, between October 2023 and August 2025 through community-based outreach. Median age was 60 (IQR 51-68) years, 155 of 182 (85.2%) participants were women, and the median number of chronic conditions was 3 (IQR 1-3). The initial 6-month digital intervention delivered brief daily modules targeting physical activity, nutrition, stress regulation, sleep, habit formation, and social connection, followed by a 6-month lower-intensity maintenance period during which monthly group videoconference sessions continued to be offered. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Primary outcomes were illness perceptions (Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire), perceived stress (10-item Perceived Stress Scale [PSS-10]), disease-related worry (10-item Questionnaire on Distress in Cancer Patients), life satisfaction (Satisfaction With Life Scale), and mental well-being (World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]). Secondary outcomes assessed the physical, behavioral, and psychosocial domains. Generalized estimating equations estimated population-averaged longitudinal changes, adjusted for age, sex, relationship status, comorbidity burden, and baseline depression or anxiety medication use. Exploratory models examined co-occurring changes and moderation. Tests were 2-sided with α =.05.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Across outcomes and follow-up assessments, completion ranged from 58.2% (95% CI 51.0%-65.2%; 106/182) to 65.4% (95% CI 58.2%-71.9%; 119/182). At 12 months, illness perceptions decreased (β=-7.3, 95% CI -9.7 to -4.9), perceived stress decreased (β=-2.4, 95% CI -3.5 to -1.3), disease-related worry decreased (β=-6.3, 95% CI -7.8 to -4.7), life satisfaction increased (β=2.5, 95% CI 1.4-3.5), and mental well-being increased (β=10.4, 95% CI 7.2-13.5; all P <.001). Secondary outcomes improved across fatigue, sleep, diet quality, sedentary behavior, spiritual well-being, mental health-related quality of life, weight, and BMI. Exploratory analyses showed that improvements in fatigue, sleep quality, and illness perceptions co-occurred with greater well-being and life satisfaction and lower perceived stress and disease-related worry at both follow-up assessment points. Clinically meaningful stress improvement (≥4-point PSS-10 reduction) was achieved by 36.4% (95% CI 27.3%-45.6%, 39/107) and 43.4% (95% CI 34.0%-52.8%, 46/106) participants at 6 and 12 months, respectively. At 12 months, 43.5% (95% CI 34.2%-52.9%, 47/108) participants reported clinically meaningful improvement in mental well-being (≥10-point WHO-5 increase).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Participation in this low-bandwidth, home-based digital self-management program was associated with sustained psychological, physical, and behavioral improvements among rural adults with chronic conditions. These multidomain findings support randomized controlled evaluation of scalable digital self-management approaches as adjuncts to rural chronic disease care.

items.title: The hidden mental health burden of corruption in healthcare: Findings from a scoping review and key informant interviews.
items.authors: Nanthakumaran M, Orjiakor C, Balabanova D.

sections.text: Corruption in healthcare is a pervasive global challenge that undermines equity, efficiency, and trust in health systems. Whilst its economic and governance impacts are well documented, the psychological consequences for patients, providers, and those involved in anti-corruption reform remain under-explored. Understanding these mental health effects is critical for designing anti-corruption strategies that safeguard wellbeing and strengthen health systems. An exploratory mixed-methods study was conducted to map an emerging evidence base. A scoping review of 25 peer-reviewed and grey literature sources was complemented by four key informant interviews, which were used to interpret and contextualise the review findings. Findings were synthesised into a conceptual framework mapping pathways between corruption and mental health outcomes. Corruption was reported to be associated with psychological distress among patients, providers, and anti-corruption actors. This included stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and moral injury. At a community level, corruption eroded trust and collective agency, whilst institutional effects included normalisation of unethical practices. Structural determinants were found to perpetuate corruption's harms. Anti-corruption efforts produced mixed outcomes: reform targeting high-level officials improved public mental health modestly, whereas punitive measures against frontline workers exacerbated fear and demoralisation in the workforce. Protective factors such as moral agency, and robust reporting systems were found to buffer harm but were context dependent. Policy recommendations are made for practice, research and capacity building. These include framing corruption as a public mental health issue, strengthening whistleblower protections, commissioning further research, and adapting reform to local political economy and social norms. These findings indicate that corruption is a plausible but under-recognised social determinant of mental health requiring further research. Integrating mental health considerations into anti-corruption policy and health system reforms is essential to mitigate harm and strengthen resilience.

items.title: Effects of a sleep program on sleep, performance and health in university students: Study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
items.authors: Andersen E, Lie Haugen F, Lindsverk H, Aasland OE, Sæther A, Bjorvatn B.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Insomnia and poor sleep are highly prevalent among university students and are linked to impaired mental and physical health, reduced cognitive functioning, and lower academic performance. Existing interventions for insomnia include cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), mindfulness, and sleep hygiene. CBT-I is widely recognised as effective but remains difficult to access for the general population and lack scalability, long-term follow-up, and feasibility in non-clinical settings. Pragmatic, group-based approaches that can be delivered within the university and are tailored to help students develop self-endorsed routines and competencies for better sleep, creating sustainable changes that extend beyond the program period, is needed.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study is a pragmatic, two-arm randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a group-based sleep program for university students with insomnia symptoms. A total of 118 full-time students aged 18-30 meeting diagnostic criteria for chronic insomnia disorder will be randomized (1:1) to either the intervention or a wait-list control group. The intervention comprises 12 weekly 90-minute group sessions followed by nine monthly follow-up meetings, facilitated by trained coaches. The program integrates core elements of CBT-I with motivational and coping strategies, delivered in an interactive and peer-supported format. The primary outcome is change in insomnia severity measured by the Bergen Insomnia Scale. Secondary outcomes include subjective and objective sleep measures, mental health, cognitive performance, academic attainment, health behaviours, physical fitness, and biological markers. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-program (12 weeks), and 12 months. A mixed methods process evaluation will assess fidelity, acceptability, mechanisms of impact, and contextual influences.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This trial will be among the first pragmatic evaluations of a structured, group-based sleep intervention tailored to university students with insomnia. Key strengths include the randomised controlled design, comprehensive outcome assessment, 12-month follow-up, and embedded process evaluation. If effective, the program could provide a feasible, scalable, and cost-effective model to improve sleep and therein health, and academic performance in young adults in higher education.

items.title: Involvement of users and caregivers in mental healthcare decision-making within low-and middle-income countries: A scoping review.
items.authors: Amos A, Jumbe S, Bandara T, Begum S, Hanlon C, Jain S, Pickersgill M, Umar E, Stewart RC.

sections.text: Inclusive healthcare decision-making is a cornerstone of recovery-oriented mental health services, contributing to improved outcomes, enhanced autonomy, and reduced stigma. While substantial research on mental healthcare decision-making has been conducted in high-income countries, there is limited evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where sociocultural norms, family structures, and health system constraints may shape decision-making differently. This review sought to synthesise evidence on service user and caregiver involvement in mental healthcare decision-making in LMICs and identify contextual factors influencing these processes. A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O'Malley's five-stage framework. English-language studies from 2008 to 2025 were identified through databases and grey literature searches. Eligible studies extracted examined the involvement of people with mental health conditions and/or caregivers in mental healthcare decision-making within LMICs. Two reviewers independently coded descriptions of involvement using an inductive content analysis approach. Three overarching themes emerged: (1) active user involvement, reflecting service users' participation in and co-creation of decisions about their care; (2) family dominance, where family members significantly influenced or controlled decision-making processes; and (3) drivers of decision-making, including cultural norms, stigma, economic hardship, social relationships, and health system constraints. Overall, decision-making was predominantly shaped by family authority and contextual factors, with relatively limited evidence of shared or supported decision-making approaches. The search yielded 21,830 records, with an additional 46 studies identified through grey literature searches. Following screening, 36 studies were included. Studies were conducted across Africa (n = 12), Asia (n = 22), and the Middle East (n = 2). Mental healthcare decision-making in LMICs is embedded within complex family, cultural, and structural contexts that both enable and constrain service user participation. This review contributes to promoting a contextualised understanding of mental healthcare decision-making in LMICs.

items.title: Experiences of Registered Nurses involved in regulatory disciplinary processes: Scoping review protocol.
items.authors: Rauman P, Devey-Burry R, Deeb A, Pike J.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The objective of this scoping review is to explore available literature on the experiences of Registered Nurses (RNs), Nurse Practitioners (NPs), and Registered Psychiatric Nurses (RPNs), who have been through the disciplinary process by the regulatory body.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Nursing is a regulated profession. Professions are regulated when there is significant risk of harm to the public if the practice is performed incorrectly. Empowered by legislation, regulatory bodies have a mandate to protect the public. This is accomplished by setting and enforcing high standards of practice and intervening when a nurse's conduct is deemed unacceptable. Existing research on disciplinary action against RNs has primarily focused on regulatory processes, predictors of misconduct, characteristics of disciplined nurses, and case outcomes across jurisdictions. However, there is a significant gap in the literature regarding the experiences of RNs have been through disciplinary proceedings. A deeper understanding of these experiences is essential to inform supportive measures for nurses during the disciplinary process and to guide improvements in regulatory policy and procedures.

sections.heading: Inclusion criteria
sections.text: This review will consider literature that includes the experiences of nurses who have gone through any component of the disciplinary process by the regulatory body. Gray literature, non-empirical, and social media (e.g., blogs) searches will be included as these sources may provide genuine and unsolicited insights into the lived experiences of nurses. Research related to the mental health of nurses, specific to disciplinary action, will be included. RNs who are regulated by entities other than a nursing regulatory body will be excluded. Research focused only on nursing disciplinary policy, procedure, outcomes or document review will be excluded, as the focus is on the lived experiences of RNs.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The JBI methodology for scoping reviews will guide the review process. A 3-step search strategy will be followed to identify published and unpublished literature in English or French with no time limit placed on the search. Data extracted from eligible literature will align with the review protocol, objectives, and research question. The results will be reported in tabular and/or diagrammatic format, accompanied by a narrative summary. OSF Review registration number: 10.17605/OSF.IO/N3SCZ.
